classification.difficultyReason: Calculate angles in the smaller and whole right triangles using different opposite lengths, then test the proposed halving relationship rather than assume midpoint implies angle bisector.

content.prompt: $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$. Determine whether the angle $\angle ACM$ is exactly half of angle $ACB$. Give calculated angles to 1 d.p.

spec.description: Triangle CAB with horizontal CA, vertical AB, midpoint M, segments CB and CM, a midpoint dot and a right-angle square at A. Ordinary source blue strokes are rendered black under house style.
spec.mathematics: CA = 6 m; AM = MB = 2 m; CA is perpendicular to AB; M is the midpoint of AB.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens are visible; no calculated angles appear in the question diagram.

answer.short: No. $\angle ACM\approx18.4^\circ$ and $\angle ACB\approx33.7^\circ$, so $\angle ACM$ is not half of $\angle ACB$.
answer.worked:
$AB=2+2=4\,\mathrm{m}$.

$$\begin{align*}
\tan\angle ACM&=\frac{AM}{AC}\\
\tan\angle ACM&=\frac{2}{6}\\
\angle ACM&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2}{6}\right)\\
\angle ACM&\approx18.43495^\circ\\
\tan\angle ACB&=\frac{AB}{AC}\\
\tan\angle ACB&=\frac{4}{6}\\
\angle ACB&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{4}{6}\right)\\
\angle ACB&\approx33.69007^\circ
\end{align*}$$

Half of $\angle ACB$ is approximately $16.84503^\circ$, which differs from $\angle ACM$. Therefore, $\angle ACM$ is not exactly half of $\angle ACB$.
